add.issue.comment.md:
Fixed, but the diagnosis in the ticket was incomplete — the suggested fixes wouldn't have worked, and I proved that by trying two of them.

Attempt 1, quantise/replace the window key: still replayed. `latest` isn't the only clock-derived value — for any scoped view `earliest` is the window *start*, which for "last 7 days" slides continuously, so the key moved anyway.

Attempt 2, fingerprint the data instead: still replayed, measured across two page loads 20s apart. A sliding window changes its start, its bucket boundaries and its contents as the clock moves, so no value derived from the fetched window can distinguish "you changed the view" from "time passed".

The deeper cause the ticket missed: the wrapper key was never the only trigger. Bars and dots were keyed by `bucket.t`, so a sliding window remounted **every mark individually**, replaying their per-element grow/twinkle animations regardless of what the wrapper did.

So two changes, both needed:
- Marks are keyed by index. They are positional slots in a fixed-count histogram — slot N is slot N — so a refetch re-styles them in place instead of tearing them down.
- The wrapper is keyed by an explicit `animationGeneration`, incremented only by things a person can do: scope, offset, board, allBoards, layout mode, and the first arrival of data.

Verified by reading React's own fiber key plus DOM node identity, since animationstart doesn't fire in a backgrounded tab (both zeros in my first run were meaningless): idle for 5s leaves the key unchanged *and* the same bar element mounted — no remount, no animation. Each user action increments exactly once: 3 -> Events 4 -> Volume 5 -> Week 6.

316 pass. Typecheck, gui:types and lint clean.

add.issue.name: Time travel: any boot() silently cancels an active checkout (contributors:get, issues:list)

edit.description.md:
`getGuiState` guards against re-materializing while scrubbed, but the guard was not hoisted, so other boot() callers still stomp the checkout.

`boot()` -> `bootStateFromEventLog` -> `materializeAll` -> `init.workspace` -> `initWorkspaceState`, whose `base` resets `readOnly: false` and `timeMode: 'live'` (source/lib/state/state.ts:132,149).

Unguarded ws handlers that boot: `contributors:get` (getBoardContributors) and `issues:list` (listIssues).

Reachable: App.tsx fires `contributors:get` from an effect keyed `[connected, selectedBoardId]`, so switching board — or a reconnect after a network blip — while scrubbed silently drops back to live. It also re-opens the websocket mutation guard, since that reads the same `getTimeTravelStatus()`.

Contradicts getGuiState's own comment ("safe by construction instead of relying on each call site to remember to guard") — these are exactly the call sites that forgot.

Fix: put the live-check inside `boot()` (or a shared read wrapper) rather than on individual entry points.

add.issue.name: Time travel: mutation guard is check-then-act across awaits, not serialized with runExclusive

edit.description.md:
websocket.ts checks `getTimeTravelStatus().mode !== 'live'` synchronously at message receipt, then the handler awaits. Same shape in api-server.ts's HTTP route guards.

`runExclusive` was added for exactly this class of bug and is used by `checkoutStateAt`, `returnToLive` and the autosync tick (9MWAGCR) — but not by the mutation handlers, so the check and the write are not atomic with respect to a scrub.

Mostly benign because `boot()` re-materializes live at the end of its own awaits, but not always: `addIssueAssignee` awaits `findEventLogAuthor` *after* boot and before `materializeAndPersistAll`. A scrub landing in that window means the assign materializes and persists against historical state.

Fix: wrap the mutating branches in `runExclusive` with the live-check inside the critical section.

add.issue.name: Redaction is undone by the event-log name override

edit.description.md:
`redactContributor` only refuses contributors who have authored no events *at the moment of redaction*. But `getLatestNamesFromLog` (epiq-api.ts) and `getContributorDisplayName` (contributor.utils.ts) let the log override the registry permanently afterwards.

So the cleared name comes back everywhere as soon as either happens:
- that userId authors any event after being redacted, or
- their per-actor log file arrives via a later `epiq_sync` (the guard only saw the logs present locally at redaction time).

The second is the realistic one for a privacy feature: redaction is workspace-wide and advertised as permanent in the modal ("it cannot be restored"), but a sync can quietly restore it.

contributor.utils.ts's "a redaction is never undone by a stale log name" is the claim that does not hold.

Fix: have the log-name override skip contributors whose registry name is `REDACTED_CONTRIBUTOR_NAME` — redaction is a forward event and should win over the log by construction, not by the guard.

add.issue.name: Redact modal offers board-scoped candidates the workspace-wide guard rejects, and swallows the failure

edit.description.md:
Two mismatched scopes:

- App.tsx sends `contributors:get` with `boardId`, so `getBoardContributors` computes `isExternal` from board-filtered events — it means "has not authored *on this board*".
- `redactContributor`'s guard uses `findEventLogAuthor` over the whole merged log — "has not authored *anywhere*".

So RedactContributorsModal shows a teammate who contributed on another board as redactable (checkbox enabled, no blockedReason), and the server then refuses.

The failure is invisible: `onRedact={ids => ids.forEach(onRedactContributor)}` fires N independent messages and `onClose()` runs immediately, and a `contributor:redact` failure only reaches App.tsx's generic `failed` branch, which does `console.log` + `requestState()`. No toast, no per-name result. Partial success across the selection is also possible with no indication of which names went through.

Fix: scope both sides the same way (pass no boardId when the list feeds the redact modal, or make the guard board-scoped), and surface per-contributor failures instead of closing unconditionally.

add.issue.name: Scrubber history buffer can commit a mismatched timeline/commits pair

edit.description.md:
`commitHistoryIfComplete` treats "both slots filled" as proof the pair belongs to one request, and the comment argues request ids are therefore unnecessary. They are not, because `requestBoardHistory` clears `pendingHistoryRef` on each new request.

Interleaving that breaks it (easy to hit by clicking through scope buttons):
1. request A sent
2. `timeline` A arrives -> buffer {timeline: A}
3. scope changes -> request B sent, buffer cleared
4. `commits` A arrives -> buffer {commits: A}
5. `timeline` B arrives -> buffer complete -> setHistory({timeline: B, commits: A})

The chart then renders B's event timeline against A's commits, and `commits` B lands in an empty buffer and is never committed — so it stays wrong until the next request.

Fix: tag requests with an incrementing id echoed in the reply (or stamp the buffer with the requested window and drop replies that don't match).

add.issue.name: Commit-diff editor spawn interpolates repo filenames into a shell string (command injection)

edit.description.md:
`openCommitAsSideBySideDiffs` derives temp paths from repo-controlled filenames (`path.basename(filePath)`, from `git diff-tree --name-only`). Those flow into `buildEditorDiffCommand`, which builds a string, and `trySpawnCommand` runs it with `spawn(cmd, {shell: true})`.

Double quotes do not stop `$(...)` or backticks, and git does not quote `$`/backtick in paths by default (core.quotePath only covers non-ASCII/control chars). Verified locally: a basename of `a$(id -u).ts` through the same quoting expands to `a503.ts` — the substitution ran.

Trigger is clicking a commit dot on the scrubber (`commit:inspect`) for a commit touching a file with such a name, so it fires on checking out and browsing any untrusted branch.

`isPlausibleSha` shows argv injection was already considered for the sha — this path was missed. `buildEditorCommand` shares the pattern but is only ever handed a ulid-named temp file, so it is not currently exploitable.

Fix: spawn with an argv array (no `shell: true`) rather than composing a shell string.

add.issue.name: TUI resolves assignee names with a full event-log scan per assignee per render

edit.description.md:
`getContributorDisplayName` (contributor.utils.ts) walks `eventLog` backwards and `isExternalContributor` (Assignee.tsx) does `eventLog.some(...)` — both per assignee, per component, on every Ink render.

The worst case is the common one: an external contributor never matches, so both scan the entire log with no early exit — and external assignees are exactly what the `↗` marker exists to show. Called from AssigneeUI, BreadCrumb's width measurement and TicketListItemCompact, so it multiplies by visible tickets on every keystroke.

The server side already establishes the right pattern for this — `getLatestNamesFromLog` builds the map once, with the comment "computed once per listing rather than per ticket". The TUI path doesn't follow it.

Fix: derive a memoised `Map<userId, {name, hasAuthored}>` from the log (invalidated on eventLog change) and read from it in the render paths.

add.issue.name: TUI unassign doesn't mirror assign's contributor resolution

edit.description.md:
`assign` (commands.ts) was reworked to resolve through `getAssignableContributors` — registry ∪ event-log authors — and to refuse when a name matches more than one contributor, so it can't silently pick the wrong person.

`unassign` still resolves with `findContributorByName`, which is `Object.values(contributors).find(c => c.name === name)`. With two contributors sharing a display name it takes the first and unassigns whichever that happens to be — the exact case assign now refuses.

`me` was added to unassign, so the two paths are half-aligned; the duplicate-name half wasn't.

Fix: resolve unassign through the same helper and return the same ambiguity failure.

add.issue.name: Repos that ran the lowercased-userId build keep orphaned contributor records

edit.description.md:
Follow-up to B4KZNAD. The fix canonicalises the actor id parsed from the log *file name*, but `create.contributor` payloads already written to the log are replayed as-is.

While the bug was live, `ensureContributorExists` minted contributor records keyed by the lowercased `event.userId`. Those records are still in the log and still materialise with lowercase ids, which now match no event userId at all.

Effects on an existing repo:
- the record is never found by `getLatestNamesFromLog` / `authorIds`, so `isExternal` is true — a real teammate renders with the `↗` external marker
- being "external" also makes them selectable in the redact modal
- assignments made under the lowercase id still point at that orphaned record, so it can't just be dropped

Worth deciding explicitly whether to migrate (emit a merge/alias event) or accept it. Flagging because the branch's own external/redact rules are derived from exactly this comparison.

add.issue.name: Timeline min/max spread unbounded arrays

edit.description.md:
`Math.min(...allTimes)` in getEventTimeline (epiq-time-travel.ts) and `Math.min(...commitTimes)` / `Math.max(...)` in TimeScrubber spread one argument per event/commit.

Unbounded in the "All time" scope, where the arrays are every event in the log and every commit in the repo. Engines cap argument count (roughly ~100k), so a large enough repo throws RangeError rather than degrading.

Fix: reduce instead of spread.

add.issue.name: Review: fix stale and misplaced comments from the time-travel/assignees branch

edit.description.md:
Pre-merge review pass over feature/time-travel. Comments that were wrong, over-claimed, or attached to the wrong declaration, plus one under-typed payload.

- App.tsx: "Held as one value, not two…" sat above `contributors` but describes `history`. Moved and trimmed.

- contributor.utils.ts + epiq-api.ts: "a redaction is never undone by a stale log name" was the overclaim behind the redaction bug.
- epiq-api.ts getGuiState: "safe by construction instead of relying on each call site to remember to guard" is contradicted by the unguarded boot() callers.
- event-load.ts: 11-line ULID rationale trimmed to 8.
- websocket.model.ts: `timeline:get` didn't declare `boardId`, which the client sends and the server forwards.

Where a comment documented an assumption the review disproved, it now carries a short KNOWN BUG note pointing at the ticket rather than quietly dropping the reasoning.

Comments only — no behaviour change. Tests (316), typecheck and prettier pass.

add.issue.name: e2e suite is flaky under parallel load

edit.description.md:
Running the full `test:e2e:ci` four times gave three different results: reboot.e2e failed, then lifecycle.e2e failed, then reboot.e2e again, then all 10 passed. Every failing test passes on its own.

Failures look like the TUI not having rendered yet when an assertion runs — e.g. `expect(output).toContain('This folder is not an epiq project yet.')` after `tui.waitFor('Initialize project', 8_000)`.

Seven e2e files run in parallel, each driving a real TUI through tmux, so the 8s waits are competing for CPU. This makes the pre-push hook fail for reasons unrelated to the change being pushed, which trains people to reach for `--no-verify`.

Options: run e2e files serially (`--no-file-parallelism` or a vitest pool setting), or scale the waitFor budgets. Serial is probably right — these are wall-clock-bound, not CPU-bound, so the parallelism buys little.

add.issue.name: Scatterplot: segment block only highlights when hovering a data point

edit.description.md:
In the scatterplot view (`layoutMode === 'real'`, the "Events" toggle) the background block marking the calendar time segment only appears while the pointer is over an actual data point. It should appear whenever the pointer is anywhere in that segment's region.

Cause: TimeScrubber.tsx binds the wrapper's `onMouseMove`/`onMouseLeave` only in `'even'` mode — in `'real'` mode they are explicitly `undefined`, so `hoveredBucketIndex` is set solely by the individual points' `onMouseEnter`. The comment there reasons that "a scatter has no column to fall into", which is the assumption to revisit: the *segment* is still a region with a start and end on the x axis, whether or not a point happens to sit under the cursor.

Fix direction: resolve the segment from the pointer's x position in both modes (`bucketIndexFromEvent` already does this arithmetically), and let the points keep their own handlers for the per-point tooltip. Sparse regions with no data should still light up their segment — the empty stretch is meaningful information in a fixed-bucket timeline.

Check the needle and tooltip stay correct in scatter mode once the wrapper handler is live, since they read the same hovered state.

add.issue.comment.md:
Better evidence — my "parallel load" diagnosis was incomplete. Stressing a single file in isolation (`peek.e2e`) still failed 2 of 12 runs, so parallelism only raises the rate, it isn't the cause.

Every observed failure is the same one, in the shared `init()` helper that all e2e tests run first:

```
e2e-common-steps.ts:37
  output = await tui.waitFor('Initialize project', 8_000);
  expect(output).toContain('This folder is not an epiq project yet.');
```

That's why the failing file moves around (peek, init, reboot, lifecycle) — it's not those tests, it's startup. The TUI sometimes takes longer than 8s to paint its first screen, or `waitFor` returns a frame captured before the paint.

So the fix is at the helper, not the scheduler: make `init()` wait on the rendered text rather than a fixed budget, or raise/scale that budget. Serialising the files is still worth doing to cut the rate, but on its own it will not remove this.

add.issue.name: Redaction guard reads unsynced local state, and redaction has no inverse

edit.description.md:
`redactContributor` refuses anyone who has authored events, but evaluates that against `boot({pull: false})` — deliberately local-only state. On a distributed board that is a stale read.

Sequence:
1. Teammate B authors events; their log file has not been pulled yet.
2. A opens the modal. B has no local events, so `hasAuthoredAnywhere` is false and B is offered as clearable.
3. A redacts B. `redact.contributor` is appended.
4. Next sync brings B's events in.

Now B is a redacted author — precisely the state the guard exists to prevent. And per TSNBNWB the `redacted` flag beats the log *unconditionally*, so B's name is cleared everywhere while the log is full of it.

Compounding: there is no `unredact.contributor` event, and the modal states "it cannot be restored". So a redaction taken on stale data is permanent.

Options:
- Require a successful `sync()` immediately before the guard runs (breaks the pull:false rule only for this one deliberate action), or surface "last synced N ago" in the modal.
- Add an inverse event so a mistake is recoverable. Cheap, append-only, and makes the stale-read case survivable rather than fatal.

add.issue.name: Redaction is not enforced on clients running an older epiq

edit.description.md:
`decodeReconstructedEvents` skips actions it doesn't recognise — correct forward-compat, and it means adding `redact.contributor` cannot brick an older client. But the flip side: an older client replays `create.contributor` (which carries the original name) and never applies the redaction, so it keeps rendering the cleared name indefinitely.

The manage-contributors modal claims the change "clears the name everywhere, on every board, for everyone" and "cannot be restored". Both are only true once every client has upgraded — which for a git-synced distributed board is never guaranteed.

Not a code defect, but the copy overstates the guarantee. Either soften it to say what is actually true (clients on an older epiq will keep showing the name until they upgrade), or gate redaction behind a minimum schema/version signal.

add.issue.name: Failed checkout leaves state wiped but reported as live and writable

edit.description.md:
`checkoutStateAt` and `returnToLive` both call `resetState()` *before* `materializeAll`, and on materialize failure return early without patching:

```
const resetResult = resetState();          // state now = initial workspace only
const materializeResults = materializeAll(appliedEvents);
if (materializeFailures.length > 0) return failed(...);   // no restore
patchState({readOnly: true, timeMode: 'peek', ...});
```

`resetState` -> `initWorkspaceState` resets `readOnly: false` / `timeMode: 'live'`, so after a failure:
- the singleton holds only the initial workspace (all boards/issues gone),
- `getTimeTravelStatus()` reports `live`, so every mutation guard opens,
- `currentAsOfTime` keeps its previous value, so status is inconsistent if an earlier checkout had succeeded.

`deriveGuiState()` has no `boot()` by design, so the broadcast path would publish a near-empty board as live. It does self-heal on the next `getGuiState()`/`boot()`, which limits the blast radius — but the failure path should restore live state explicitly rather than depend on the next caller.

The existing test `fails without patching state when materialization fails` pins `patchState` not being called, which is the safe half; it doesn't cover the wiped-state consequence. Worth extending to assert the state is usable afterwards.

add.issue.name: addIssueAssignee's name path ignores event-log authors, unlike TUI and picker
Post-mutation state broadcast escapes the time-travel lock

edit.description.md:
ZSQ8ZQ5 put mutating handlers inside `runExclusive`, but `sendMutationResult` ends with a deliberate fire-and-forget:

```
void sendGuiState(socket, repoRoot);
```

That resolves *after* the lock is released, so its `getGuiState()` snapshot is not ordered against a `time-travel:scrub` queued right behind the mutation. A client can receive one `state` broadcast that disagrees with the checkout it just entered.

Low severity: nothing is persisted, `bootStateFromEventLog`'s guard prevents the checkout itself from being stomped, and the next interaction corrects the view. Noting it so the "everything is serialised" claim in the surrounding comments isn't read as covering this path too.

Fix is either awaiting the broadcast inside the lock (costs the requester latency the comment was avoiding) or having it re-check `getTimeTravelStatus()` and use `deriveGuiState()` when not live.

Opening a ticket navigates from `/board/:boardId` to `/board/:boardId/issue/:issueId`, and the timeline re-renders and replays its entrance every time. It should stay put: while `boardId` is unchanged there is no new window to draw.

Where to look:

`main.tsx` declares four routes that each render their own `<App />`:

```
<Route path="/" element={<App />} />
<Route path="/board/:boardId" element={<App />} />
<Route path="/board/:boardId/issue/:issueId" element={<App />} />
<Route path="/board/:boardId/:issueId" element={<App />} />
```

So every selection switches which route matches. A quick probe showed a **second WebSocket being constructed right after selecting a ticket**, which points at `<App />` remounting rather than re-rendering — its socket effect is keyed `[boardId]` and boardId does not change, so a re-run implies a fresh mount. If App does remount, the blast radius is wider than the timeline: all App state resets on every ticket click, including `pickedIssueIds`, which would explain multi-select appearing to drop the first ticket (GQX4Z92).

Likely direction: one route element with optional params, or a layout route wrapping a shared `<App />`, so navigation changes params without swapping the element.

Note `windowKey` in TimeScrubber is already keyed to the arrived history window (YFNMZYS), so once remounting stops the animation should not replay on a plain sync — worth re-checking after.

edit.description.md:
Hover and drag write React state on every pointer event. A mouse fires well above 60/s, so the scrubber re-renders more often than the screen refreshes and most of those renders are discarded.

NCFA2DX cut the cost of each render (29.8ms -> 8.2ms median); this cuts how many happen at all.

- without:            4.1ms total, 0.1ms median burst
- same build 4x:      4.2 / 5.4 / 4.6 / 5.5ms

edit.description.md:

Needs a **minute** segment unit as well. `chooseSegmentUnit` takes the finest unit giving ≤ `MAX_SEGMENTS` (35) and its finest is `hour`, so a one-hour span resolves to a single segment and the hover highlight covers the whole track — the same degeneracy AN77QXR called out for Day.

Raising `MAX_SEGMENTS` is not the fix: at 60 the year view flips from month segments to week segments (365/7 = 52 ≤ 60). Every other scope is unaffected either way.

add.issue.name: The punchcard y axis is meaningless at the hour scope

An hour-wide window spans at most two adjacent hours, so every dot lands inside ~4% of the height — a thin band under an axis claiming a full day. The volume layout is unaffected; only the scatter degrades.

Options:

**A. Leave it.** Not strictly wrong — time of day really is near-constant inside an hour — but it looks broken and the axis labels lie about what is shown.

**B. Make the cycle follow the scope.** Under a day-wide span, y becomes minute-of-hour, labelled :00 / :30 / :59. Keeps the punchcard's premise — x is elapsed time, y is position in a repeating cycle — and only changes which cycle. Mirrors the segment unit stepping finer, which N8CH4ZX already does.

**C. Flatten the scatter for fine scopes.** Drop y entirely under a day and draw a strip. Cheapest, loses the second dimension.

Leaning B, but it reaches `hourFractionForTime` (used by TimeScrubber and ScrubberLayout) and turns `HourAxisLabels` from a constant into something that takes the span — wider than "add an hour scope", so not doing it unasked.

edit.description.md:
Confirmed, but the cause is narrower than the original title assumed, and no git operation is involved.

TUI, GUI and MCP all read and write the *same* state branch worktree, so there is nothing to "fetch from the local state branch" — the sibling session's events are already on disk.

- **TUI already works with no remote.** `syncAndReloadStateUnsafe` reloads via `loadMergedEvents` unconditionally after `syncEpiqWithRemote`, pulled or not.

It only looks fine with a remote because `pullBranchRebaseIfPresent` returns `true` whenever the remote branch exists, regardless of whether anything came down — the gate degenerates to always-broadcast, which also clobbers clients more often than intended.

The gate exists to avoid replacing every client's board wholesale mid-edit, so it should ask whether the **loaded state changed** (edge event id / event count since the last broadcast) rather than what the sync did. That is remote-independent and cuts the needless clobbering.

add.issue.name: Sync wedges permanently after a conflicted state-branch rebase

edit.description.md:
A single actor writing from two clones diverges textually on their own `.jsonl`. `pull --rebase` then conflicts, and two things break at once:

1. Git leaves `<<<<<<<` markers in the file. `parsePersistedEventsFile` fails on `JSON.parse`, so `loadMergedEvents` fails and **TUI, GUI and MCP all fail to load the board** — including time-travel reads, which share the path via `loadMergedEventsBefore`.
2. `.git/worktrees/<id>/rebase-merge` survives. Every later `syncEpiqWithRemote` fails at `ensureSyncReady`'s `hasInProgressGitOperation` guard — **before** `pullBranchRebaseIfPresent`'s `abortRebaseIfPresent` can run. Sync stays wedged until a human runs `git rebase --abort` in `~/.epiq-global/worktrees/<projectId>`.

So the recovery already written into the pull path is unreachable, because the guard in front of it rejects first.

Direction: abort a stale state-branch rebase inside `ensureSyncReady` before that guard rejects, so sync self-heals. The guard must still reject a genuinely concurrent operation — the distinction is a leftover from our own failed pull vs. something running right now.

Found while confirming SKZYP5Q. Pairs with the union merge driver ticket, which removes the conflict at the source; this one makes an already-wedged repo recover.

add.issue.name: Give the per-actor event logs a union merge driver

edit.description.md:
Per-actor files make conflicts impossible *across* actors, but not for one actor writing from two clones — laptop and desktop both append to `<userId>.<userName>.jsonl` and `pull --rebase` conflicts textually.

Fix it at the source: a `.gitattributes` carrying `*.jsonl merge=union`, so git concatenates both sides instead of conflicting.

Constraints:

- It must live **inside `.epiq/`** (e.g. `.epiq/events/.gitattributes`). `ensureStateBranchIsStorageOnly` `git rm`s anything at the state-branch root that is not `.epiq`, so a root-level file would be deleted and committed away on the next sync.
- Union merge is safe for ordering here. File line order is not load-bearing: `getSortedEvents` rebuilds order causally from `id[1]` (the edge ref at write time) and dedupes by event id, so duplicated or interleaved lines resolve to the same state.
- Cross-version: the attribute only changes how a client's *own* git merges, so a client on an older epiq that fetches the branch before this lands is unaffected either way. Nothing about the event format changes.

Prerequisite reading: the wedge ticket, which handles repos that have already conflicted — the driver only prevents new ones.

add.issue.name: A schema-version bump kills the board on older clients

edit.description.md:
Forward compatibility is asymmetric, and the unsafe half is the one that takes the whole board down.

Unknown **actions** degrade gracefully — `decodeReconstructedEvents` skips them, logs once ("likely created by a newer epiq version"), and leaves the persisted files untouched.

Unknown **schema versions** do not. `PersistedEventSchema` is `z.looseObject({v: z.literal(1), …})`, so a single `v: 2` line makes `parsePersistedEvent` fail → `parsePersistedEventsFile` fail → `loadAllPersistedEvents` fail. The older client cannot load the board at all, and neither can it time travel: `loadMergedEventsBefore` shares the path.

One teammate upgrading is enough to brick everyone who has not — the moment their events reach a shared state branch.

Direction: make an unrecognised `v` behave like an unrecognised action. Skip the line, count it, log once, never rewrite the file. That keeps the old client usable on the subset it understands and keeps the newer events intact for when it upgrades — same contract `isKnownEventAction` already sets.

`source/lib/event/event-persist.ts`, `source/lib/event/event-load.ts`. Note the skip has to happen per line, not per file, or one new event still costs the whole actor's log.

add.issue.name: Scrubber period label drops the time when the scope is Hour

edit.description.md:
With scope **Hour** and the period stepped back, the label reads `8/22 – 8/22` — both ends land on the same calendar day, so it carries no information at all. It should show the hourly span.

`formatPeriodLabel` (`source/gui/client/lib/scrubber.ts`) formats every non-`all` scope the same way once `offset !== 0`:

```
`${start.getMonth() + 1}/${start.getDate()} – ${end.getMonth() + 1}/${end.getDate()}`
```

Date-only, regardless of scope. Hour is the degenerate case; `day` is nearly as weak, since a rolling 24h window prints two adjacent dates with no clue where inside them it sits.

Only visible after paging back — at `offset === 0` the label comes from `SCOPE_RECENT_LABELS` ("Last hour"), which is why the default view looks fine.

The nearby segment-tick formatter in the same file already solves this: it switches format by unit and renders an hour as `Wed 14:00`. Worth reusing that shape rather than adding a second convention — the label and the ticks below it should agree.

Note the ranges are rolling windows ending now (`getPeriodRange` subtracts `offset * durationMs` from `Date.now()`), not calendar periods, so an hour window is rarely aligned to `:00` — the format has to read sensibly for e.g. `14:37 – 15:37`.

- `parsePersistedEventsFile` validates the envelope only and **retains every well-formed line**, whatever its version. A malformed envelope is still genuine corruption and still fails the load.
- The version skip moved to `decodeReconstructedEvents`, next to the unknown-action skip — i.e. after ordering and anchoring have already run. That is where unknown actions were always handled, so the two are now genuinely symmetric.

add.issue.name: The stable event envelope has a closed id tuple, so extending id bricks old clients

edit.description.md:

add.issue.name: stop treating every materialization failure as fatal

edit.description.md:
`bootStateFromEventLog` fails the whole boot if any event fails to materialize:

```ts
const failures = results.filter(isFail);
if (failures.length > 0) return failed(`Materializing failed:\n...`);
```

The materializers are partial, not total — roughly 30 `materializeFail` sites, most of them preconditions ("Unable to locate node X", "Cannot edit readonly node", "missing contributor", "missing target"). Skipping an event, which is exactly what an unknown action or a concurrent edit causes, is what makes those preconditions untrue.

So a merge can produce a log that does not boot. Worse, it inverts who pays: the client that skipped the event is fine, while the client that understands *both* events is the one that cannot open the board. And it is permanent, because the log is append-only.

Demonstrated: `tombstone.contributor c1` followed by `rename.contributor c1` returns
`Materializing failed: rename contributor failed, cannot rename a removed contributor`.

## The split

- **Convergence failures** — ordering and preconditions. The event lost a race, or refers to state this replay does not have. Skip it and keep going; tombstone-wins and delete-wins fall out naturally.
- **Corruption failures** — invalid user id, malformed rank, bad payload. The log is genuinely broken. Still fatal.

Both currently go through the same `materializeFail`, so the distinction does not exist anywhere. Work is: give it a category, triage every site (each needs a real decision — no-op, or which side wins), and make boot fatal only on the corruption class.

## Consequences

- Silent divergence becomes possible: two clients can hold different state with nothing saying so. Needs to be visible — a count of events that could not be applied, surfaced rather than swallowed.
- Once replay is total, the board-wide unreadable lock is no longer load-bearing for ordering, and `RETIRED_EVENT_ACTIONS` goes away with it. Remove those two **together and last** — deleting the retired list before this work re-locks boards that carry an abandoned action.

add.issue.name: never auto-commit in the user's repo — only the state branch

edit.description.md:
Autosync creates commits in the user's own repository. Observed twice in one session on this repo: a commit titled "Initial commit" appeared unbidden, the second time capturing 17 staged files of unrelated work.

epiq owns the state branch worktree. It has no business writing commits in a repo that may hold unrelated or confidential work in progress. The exposure is not "a stray commit", it is arbitrary staged content captured into a commit nobody wrote.

## Chain

`startGuiAutoSync` runs `sync()` on a timer (15s here) -> `sync.ts:245` calls `ensureInitialCommit(repoRoot)` — the user's repo, not the state worktree -> guard misfires -> `git commit --allow-empty -m 'Initial commit'` with **no pathspec**, sweeping in whatever is staged.

Verified NOT affected: pushing. `pushStateBranch` always runs with `cwd: stateBranchRoot`, so only `__epiq_state__` is pushed and the stray commits stayed local.

## Three defects

1. **Reachable from sync at all.** `ensureInitialCommit` belongs on the `:init` path only, where the user explicitly asked to set the project up. It exists for a real reason — creating the state branch needs a commit to branch from — but that is a one-time, input-sourced bootstrap.
2. **Fails open.** `rev-parse --verify HEAD` exits non-zero for "no HEAD" *and* for "the command failed": a 10s timeout gives `exitCode: 124`, a spawn error or missing cwd gives `1`. Any of those currently reads as "empty repo". If we cannot positively confirm the repo has no commits, do nothing.
3. **Captures the index.** `--allow-empty` only permits an empty diff, it does not force one, so the commit takes whatever is staged. Use plumbing (`commit-tree` on the empty tree, then `update-ref`) so it is structurally incapable of committing user content.

(3) matters most: with plumbing, a future caller who gets the guard wrong still cannot take the user's files.

Consider also a shared assertion that no commit helper is invoked with `cwd === repoRoot` outside init, so this cannot regress quietly.

Workaround until fixed: `autoSync: false`, or do not leave the GUI running with staged work.

error: please commit or stash them.

add.issue.name: Scrub without re-materializing the board from scratch

edit.description.md:
Every scrub throws the board away and rebuilds it from event zero. After the per-replay batching in `3XACRX` a scrub is ~150ms on this repo (1992 events); the remaining cost is almost entirely `materializeAll`, and it grows with the log.

## Where it lives

`checkoutStateAt` in `source/mcp/epiq-time-travel.ts` does, per scrub:

1. `resolveStateBranchRoot`
2. `loadMergedEventsBefore(root, targetTime)` — reads and decodes **every** event file from disk, twice (applied + unapplied). ~20ms
3. `resetState()`
4. `materializeAll(appliedEvents)` — ~144ms
5. `patchState({readOnly: true, timeMode: 'peek', unappliedEvents, replay: null})`, then sets the module-level `currentAsOfTime`

The websocket handler (`source/gui/api/lib/websocket.ts`, `time-travel:scrub`) then calls `broadcastDerivedState()`.

**Do not spend time on the broadcast.** Measured: derive 1.5ms, slim 0.1ms, stringify 0.3ms for a 117KB payload. It is not the cost.

## Plan

**Step 1 — cache the decoded log.** Hold the decoded events in a module-level cache instead of re-reading and re-decoding per scrub. Key it on something that changes when the log does: the state branch HEAD sha (`git rev-parse HEAD` in the state worktree) plus the event dir mtimes, or invalidate explicitly from the sync path. Autosync writes events between scrubs, so a stale cache is the main hazard. Worth ~20ms and it is the prerequisite for step 2.

**Step 2 — step forward instead of resetting.** Keep the events already applied and the current `currentAsOfTime`. When the new target is *later*, apply only the events in `(currentAsOfTime, target]` with no `resetState()`. When it is *earlier*, fall back to the current reset-and-replay. Scrubbing drags in both directions, so this removes roughly half the work for free.

**Step 3 — only if steps 1–2 are not enough.** Periodic snapshots: deep-clone state every N events and replay from the nearest snapshot at or before the target, which also makes backward moves cheap. Measure the clone cost and memory before committing to it — this is the expensive option and may not be worth it.

## Constraints

- Nothing reads the event logs or ticket virtual nodes *during* materialization (only API-level code does), which is what made the `3XACRX` batching safe. Re-verify if you change what materialize does.
- `unappliedEvents` is patched into state and must stay correct on every path, including the forward-step one.
- Time travel is server-global and serialized by `runExclusive` in `epiq-time-travel.ts` — that lock is not re-entrant.
- `returnToLive` rebuilds via `materializeAll` and then `relockUnreadableEvents()`; any cache must be invalidated or reused correctly there too.

## Verification

`source/test/replay-equivalence.test.ts` is the right model and the existing guard for this area: it deep-compares a batched replay against a per-event one. Extend it so an incrementally-reached state at time T deep-equals a cold `checkoutStateAt(T)`, over a series of forward and backward targets including exact event boundaries. Confirm the new assertions actually fail when the incremental path is broken — the existing ones do.

Also run `npm run test:e2e` (docker, needs `npm run build:e2e:image`); it covers peek, replay and reboot, and is excluded from `npm test`.

## How to measure

In-process, against this repo: load events with `loadMergedEventsBefore`, `resetState()`, then time `materializeAll`.

End to end: start the GUI (`IS_LOCAL=true npx tsx source/Index.tsx gui`, read the port from its output — it falls back off 3710 if taken), connect a raw `ws` client, send `{type:'time-travel:scrub',payload:{targetTime}}` and time until `time-travel:result`. Discard the first scrub; it includes warm-up and reads ~1000ms against ~150ms steady state.

That assumption does not hold. The gate opens during render, but the request is sent from a `useEffect` and `historyBuffer.open()` runs there — so between the two, a reply still in flight for the window just left can publish, close the gate with the wrong data, and leave the real reply ignored.

edit.description.md:
Write `<userId>.jsonl` instead of `<userId>.<userName>.jsonl`. Keep reading both — existing files keep their name segment and it is simply ignored.

## Why

- **`tombstone.contributor` cannot currently do what it claims.** It clears the display name from the registry, but the name is baked into a git-tracked file name, in history, permanently. Dropping the segment means future events carry no name on disk at all.
- One file per contributor forever, instead of one per name they have ever used. A rename currently starts a new log file.
- `sanitizeFilePart` stops being semantically load-bearing and becomes what its docstring already claims: a storage encoding.

## Sequencing — the gate is now open

The reader half (ignore the name segment, resolve names from the registry) shipped in b48b746, which went out in **v1.5.0**. This is the writer half, and it had to wait for a release that clients are actually on. That release exists now, so the only remaining condition is that the people sharing this board have upgraded to 1.5.0 or later.

The hazard this sequencing avoids, for the record: a pre-b48b746 client reading `<ulid>.jsonl` parses `userName` as `'unknown'` (the file name schema's default for a missing segment). `preferBestName('Alice', 'unknown')` then re-encodes `'Alice'` to `'alice'`, mismatches, and picks the log's — so Alice displays as "unknown".

That leaks into name *matching*, not just display. In the old `addIssueAssignee`, assigning "Alice" by name finds no candidate; with `createUnlinked` — which the failure message explicitly suggests — it mints a fresh ULID and writes a `create.contributor` for a second "Alice". A duplicate identity, persisted as a real event. This is the failure `mergeRegistryNames` carries a comment warning about.

It is also asymmetric: each contributor writes their own log file, so one person upgrading degrades everyone else's view of *that person*.

## The change

- `getPersistFileName` (`source/lib/event/event-persist.ts:140`) -> `${sanitizeFilePart(userId)}.jsonl`. `stageStateBranchOwnEventFile` follows it; the `.jsonl`-doubling guard in `getEventLogPath` still holds.
- No migration needed: `parseEventFileActor` splits on the first `.` and already falls through to the `'unknown'` default when there is no separator, so it reads both forms today.
- Close a sharp edge at the same time: `findEventLogAuthor` would return `name: 'unknown'` for an id in the log but absent from the registry, and its caller writes that straight into a `create.contributor`. It should refuse `'unknown'` rather than register somebody under it. Believed unreachable now that `ensureContributorCurrent` guarantees a record for every author, but worth closing rather than relying on that.

edit.description.md:
Every scrub throws the board away and rebuilds it from event zero. The cost grows with the log.

## Re-measure before doing anything

The numbers below were taken after `3XACRX` and before `PAM6JK2`, which landed straight after and disabled ticket virtual fields outside the TUI — 112–128ms of the ~130ms `materializeAll` those numbers attribute to it, in exactly the GUI process this ticket is about.

So the premise "the remaining cost is almost entirely `materializeAll`" is stale, and step 2 may now be optimising the wrong thing. Re-measure a GUI scrub first. If `materializeAll` has dropped to a few tens of ms, the ~20ms decode in step 1 is the dominant cost and step 1 alone may close this.

Numbers as they stood after `3XACRX` (1992 events): scrub ~150ms, of which `materializeAll` ~144ms.

## Where it lives

`checkoutStateAt` in `source/mcp/epiq-time-travel.ts` does, per scrub:

1. `resolveStateBranchRoot`
2. `loadMergedEventsBefore(root, targetTime)` — reads and decodes **every** event file from disk, twice (applied + unapplied). ~20ms
3. `resetState()`
4. `materializeAll(appliedEvents)`
5. `patchState({readOnly: true, timeMode: 'peek', unappliedEvents, replay: null})`, then sets the module-level `currentAsOfTime`

The websocket handler (`source/gui/api/lib/websocket.ts`, `time-travel:scrub`) then calls `broadcastDerivedState()`.

**Do not spend time on the broadcast.** Measured: derive 1.5ms, slim 0.1ms, stringify 0.3ms for a 117KB payload. It is not the cost.

## Plan

**Step 1 — cache the decoded log.** Hold the decoded events in a module-level cache instead of re-reading and re-decoding per scrub. Key it on something that changes when the log does: the state branch HEAD sha (`git rev-parse HEAD` in the state worktree) plus the event dir mtimes, or invalidate explicitly from the sync path. Autosync writes events between scrubs, so a stale cache is the main hazard. Likely the biggest remaining win now, and the prerequisite for step 2 either way.

**Step 2 — step forward instead of resetting.** Keep the events already applied and the current `currentAsOfTime`. When the new target is *later*, apply only the events in `(currentAsOfTime, target]` with no `resetState()`. When it is *earlier*, fall back to the current reset-and-replay. Scrubbing drags in both directions, so this removes roughly half the work for free. Value depends entirely on what the re-measure says `materializeAll` still costs.

**Step 3 — only if steps 1–2 are not enough.** Periodic snapshots: deep-clone state every N events and replay from the nearest snapshot at or before the target, which also makes backward moves cheap. Measure the clone cost and memory before committing to it — this is the expensive option and may not be worth it.

## Constraints

- Nothing reads the event logs or ticket virtual nodes *during* materialization (only API-level code does), which is what made the `3XACRX` batching safe. Re-verify if you change what materialize does.
- `unappliedEvents` is patched into state and must stay correct on every path, including the forward-step one.
- Time travel is server-global and serialized by `runExclusive` in `epiq-time-travel.ts` — that lock is not re-entrant.
- `returnToLive` rebuilds via `materializeAll`; any cache must be invalidated or reused correctly there too.

## Verification

`source/test/replay-equivalence.test.ts` is the right model and the existing guard for this area: it deep-compares a batched replay against a per-event one. Extend it so an incrementally-reached state at time T deep-equals a cold `checkoutStateAt(T)`, over a series of forward and backward targets including exact event boundaries. Confirm the new assertions actually fail when the incremental path is broken — the existing ones do.

Also run `npm run test:e2e` (docker, needs `npm run build:e2e:image`); it covers peek, replay and reboot, and is excluded from `npm test`.

## How to measure

In-process, against this repo: load events with `loadMergedEventsBefore`, `resetState()`, then time `materializeAll`. Note this path has virtual nodes **on**, unlike the GUI server — see `setVirtualNodesEnabled` — so it no longer reflects what a real scrub costs.

End to end, which does: start the GUI (`IS_LOCAL=true npx tsx source/Index.tsx gui`, read the port from its output — it falls back off 3710 if taken), connect a raw `ws` client, send `{type:'time-travel:scrub',payload:{targetTime}}` and time until `time-travel:result`. Discard the first scrub; it includes warm-up.

edit.description.md:
Hit live during the v1.5.0 board sweep, on the first `epiq_sync` after a batch of MCP writes:

```
Failed during pull --rebase
git -c rebase.autoStash=true pull --rebase origin __epiq_state__
From https://github.com/ljtn/epiq
 * branch              __epiq_state__ -> FETCH_HEAD
fatal: Cannot rebase onto multiple branches.
```

An immediate retry succeeded, so it is a race, not a wedge.

`pullBranchRebaseIfPresent` runs `pull --rebase` with an explicit refspec. `pull` fetches into `FETCH_HEAD` and then rebases onto what it finds there. Git emits this exact fatal when `FETCH_HEAD` holds more than one mergeable entry — which is what a second fetch into the same worktree produces if it lands between our fetch and our rebase.

The state-branch worktree is shared: a running GUI's autosync, a TUI session and an MCP call all sync through it, on timers. So two `pull`s overlapping is the normal case, not an exotic one, and `FETCH_HEAD` is the shared mutable file they collide on.

Direction: stop depending on `FETCH_HEAD`. Fetch into the remote-tracking ref and rebase onto that by name (`git fetch origin __epiq_state__:refs/remotes/origin/__epiq_state__`, then `git rebase origin/__epiq_state__`) — a named ref is not clobbered by a concurrent fetch the way `FETCH_HEAD` is. `P4QTPMR` already moved the pull path toward reading the remote-tracking ref locally, so this follows the same line.

Serialising sync across processes would also close it, but that is a much bigger change than removing the `FETCH_HEAD` dependency.

Neighbours: `BZJR3VE` (a rebase that conflicts wedges sync permanently) and `55NWR3D` (the union merge driver that stops it conflicting). This one is upstream of both — the rebase here never started.

add.issue.name: A test run rewrote the developer's branches and git identity

edit.description.md:
Running the suites from a git worktree located **inside** the main checkout (`.claude/worktrees/<name>`) corrupted the real repository:

- `main` was moved off `origin/main` onto a chain of test commits — `base`, `seed`, `initial`, `real work`, `no pathspec`, `test commit`, `[epiq:init-project]`
- `user.name=Test` / `user.email=test@example.com` were written into the shared `.git/config` at repo level, so every subsequent commit was misattributed
- a `MERGE_HEAD` containing `dummy` was left in `.git/worktrees/<name>/`, which blocks committing with `fatal: Corrupt MERGE_HEAD file`
- the worktree's HEAD was checked out onto `main`

Every stray commit message belongs to `git-safety.test.ts` — the suite whose stated purpose is that "epiq writes commits in the user's own repository in exactly one place".

## Not reproduced

Against a disposable clone (`git clone --no-local`), all of these were clean: `git-safety.test.ts` alone, the full unit suite, the collaboration suite, and the entire pre-push hook — run both in a normal checkout and in a worktree of it.

The one structural difference not yet tested: the worktree that got corrupted lived **inside** the parent repo's working tree, so a helper resolving a repo from `process.cwd()` can walk up into the parent, whose checked-out branch is `main`. That fits the evidence (commits landing on `main`, config written at repo level) but is unproven.

`makeRepo` in `git-safety.test.ts` guards correctly — mkdtemp, realpath, and a refusal to operate outside the temp dir — so the leak is likely a helper that takes a repo path from somewhere other than `makeRepo`.

## Mitigation already landed

The collaboration suite now runs in the e2e container with the checkout mounted **read-only** (`-v "$PWD":/app:ro`), so it cannot reach the host repository at all. The same treatment is worth extending to any suite that shells out to git.

## Still worth doing

Find the actual leak. A candidate check: assert in a global test setup that `git rev-parse --show-toplevel` from any repo a test operates on resolves under `os.tmpdir()`, and fail loudly otherwise — the guarantee `git-safety.test.ts` already claims, enforced for every suite rather than one file.

A `git push` rewrote the developer's branches and git identity:

- `main` was moved off `origin/main` onto a chain of test commits — `base`, `seed`, `initial`, `real work`, `no pathspec`, `test commit`, `[epiq:init-project]`
- `user.name=Test` / `user.email=test@example.com` were written into the shared `.git/config`, so every later commit was misattributed
- a `MERGE_HEAD` containing `dummy` was left in the git dir, which blocks committing with `fatal: Corrupt MERGE_HEAD file`
- the worktree's HEAD was checked out onto `main`

## Cause

**Git exports `GIT_DIR` into the environment of its hooks.** It overrides repository discovery, so every `git` the suite ran under `git push` was aimed at the developer's repository regardless of `cwd`.

That is why `makeRepo` in `git-safety.test.ts` did not help: it validates the *path*, and `GIT_DIR` bypasses paths entirely. Running the suites — or even `sh .husky/pre-push` — by hand never reproduces it, because only a real `git push` sets the variable.

Reproduced in a disposable clone by setting `GIT_DIR` and changing nothing else, giving the same signature: a `Test`-authored commit on the checked-out branch plus the injected identity.

Not worktree-specific. A plain checkout is equally exposed.

## Three paths were affected

1. Anything vitest runs.
2. The collaboration suite, which shells out to git heavily.
3. Playwright's `global-setup`, which spawns the GUI server on the host; it seeds by driving a real TUI, which inherited the variable.

add.issue.comment.md:
Correction to what this ticket first said: the original guess — that it was specific to a worktree living inside the parent checkout, letting a helper walk up into it — was wrong. The description now carries the real cause, `GIT_DIR`.

The reason that guess survived so long is worth recording: every attempt to reproduce it ran the suites, or `sh .husky/pre-push`, **by hand**. Only a real `git push` sets `GIT_DIR`, so the corrupting condition was never present in any of those runs. Four clean reproductions in a disposable clone all proved nothing.

Solution, in three commits:

- `source/test/setup/no-git-outside-tmp.ts` strips the variables for anything vitest runs, refuses to hand one to a child process, and fails a test that aims git at the checkout rather than a temp directory. Wired in via `setupFiles`.
- The collaboration suite runs in the e2e container with the checkout mounted read-only, so it cannot reach the host repository whether or not the cause is understood.
- Playwright's `global-setup` strips them before spawning the GUI server, which seeds by driving a real TUI. This one is invisible to the vitest guard and was the last failure standing.

The variable list is shared in `source/test/setup/git-hook-env.ts` rather than duplicated.

Verification:

- 591 unit tests pass under a real `git push` with `GIT_DIR` set; the same run previously failed 22 and corrupted the repo.
- Replaying the corrupting scenario with the fix: 14/14 pass, HEAD unchanged, no new damage.
- After a clean push: `main` still at `origin/main`, identity intact, no local overrides.
- Four tests cover the guard itself, so it cannot rot into decoration.

Left undone: `git-safety.test.ts` asserts "no commit reaches the user repository outside init" by scanning source for `cwd: repoRoot`. That is a static check and would not have caught this, since the escape needs no suspicious argument. Worth extending it to assert the environment is clean too.
